page: Amazon Web Services m1.xlarge is a first-generation general-purpose virtual machine hosted on the Xen hypervisor. The instance is provisioned with four dedicated physical cores running on an Intel Xeon E5-2651 v2 processor with an x86_64 architecture operating at a base frequency of 1.8 GHz. It is configured with 15.0 GB of system memory, providing 3.75 GB per core. The instance incorporates 1680 GB of integrated local HDD storage, lacks GPU acceleration, and operates with a 1 Gbps baseline network bandwidth profile.

Benchmark results reflect the limitations of this legacy hardware platform. The instance places in the bottom decile for compute metrics, registering a single-core Geekbench score of 496.0, a multi-core score of 1205.0, and a PassMark CPU score of 2779.52. Architectural capabilities are constrained by the absence of modern vector instruction sets such as AVX, AVX-512, and AMX, although hardware AES encryption instructions are present. Memory subsystem benchmarks show uncached read throughput of 22.53 GB/sec and write throughput of 19.35 GB/sec.

The primary operational tradeoff of the m1.xlarge is its combination of older compute performance and substantial bundled magnetic capacity. While the 1680 GB local HDD offers ample local storage density without remote volume attachment, mechanical disk latency and lower CPU throughput restrict efficiency for modern compute-bound workloads. Cost efficiency is largely confined to legacy systems specifically requiring high-capacity ephemeral disk space rather than modern processor execution.

Workload suitability for the m1.xlarge includes legacy application hosting, non-critical background batch processing, offline log retention, and basic staging servers where high-throughput CPU cycles and modern vector extensions are unnecessary.
description: Amazon Web Services m1.xlarge is a first-generation general-purpose instance featuring four dedicated cores on an Intel Xeon E5-2651 v2 processor clocked at 1.8 GHz, supported by 15.0 GB of RAM. The instance lacks specialized hardware acceleration and advanced vector instruction sets like AVX, resulting in lower-tier benchmark results such as a PassMark CPU score of 2779.52 and a Geekbench multi-core rating of 1205.0. However, it integrates 1680 GB of local HDD storage and a 1 Gbps network baseline. While cost efficiency is compromised for modern compute tasks due to older architectural standards and lower processing speeds, the large local mechanical disk volume provides dense temporary storage. This configuration suits legacy software, sequential batch processing, secondary data staging, and lightweight background services that do not rely on high-frequency execution or modern vector instructions.
